goal: Determine the smallest defensible ontology-first implementation-structure and enforcement model for DomainSpec v2, grounded in current DomainSpec precedent and projected idiomatically into initial TypeScript, Python, and Rust profiles.
context: The target spans source layout, imports, rule and meta-type organization, composability, state-machine construction, language tooling, and authority boundaries. Current DomainSpec v2 and implementation/domainspec already contain partial validators, architecture-pattern material, code-tag machinery, parser planning, and generated evidence that must be classified before proposing anything new. The result must distinguish universal DomainSpec obligations from language-specific policies and must surface blind spots, typed negatives, migration costs, and unproven claims. Research artifacts are proposal-only and may not mutate code, canonical ontology, definitions, authority records, generated projections, Git, or public Arcanum.
anti_bias_global: Composite methodology, source-corpus, and attack-vector tension across current repository precedent, ontology and authority semantics, ecosystem-native language enforcement, and adversarial non-collapse.

groups.anti_bias: Composite methodology and source-corpus axis: repository archaeology, formal ontology and authority modeling, and current ecosystem tooling comparison.

predicted_disagreements.statement: Agent 0 runs repository archaeology over current DomainSpec implementations while agent 1 runs formal ontology and authority analysis on the methodology and source-corpus axis; a bias in agent 0 toward accidental existing structure would be exposed by agent 1 when files or linters lack a governed semantic owner, while a bias in agent 1 toward elegant types would be exposed by agent 0 when the model duplicates or contradicts working repository mechanisms.

Agent 0 runs local precedent and live enforcement tracing while agent 2 runs current TypeScript, Python, and Rust tooling comparison on the methodology and source-corpus axis; a bias in agent 0 toward repo-local convention would be exposed by agent 2 when native ecosystems cannot enforce it safely, while a bias in agent 2 toward generic best practice would be exposed by agent 0 when it ignores DomainSpec authority, generated-source, or receipt constraints.

Agent 1 runs ontology-first obligation and projection modeling while agent 2 runs language-native compiler, linter, module, and state-machine analysis on the methodology and source-corpus axis; a bias in agent 1 toward cross-language uniformity would be exposed by agent 2 when it erases language idioms or tool limits, while a bias in agent 2 toward per-language convenience would be exposed by agent 1 when profiles no longer preserve the same DomainSpec obligation.

agents.angle: Repository archaeology: classify existing DomainSpec v2 and implementation/domainspec architecture, rule, validator, tag, parser, state-machine, and folder-enforcement mechanisms as active owner, generated projection, historical precedent, partial enforcement, or gap.
agents.initial_prompt: Read only the scoped local corpus under projects/domainspec-v2/, implementation/domainspec/, and the relevant Inventory packet leads. Trace current implementation conventions, package scripts, lint and validation configuration, architecture-pattern libraries/cards, code-tag composability checks, rule modules and imports, state-machine examples, parser experiment artifacts, generated sources, and receipts. For every mechanism return an exact path plus selector, authority status, what it actually enforces, bypasses/false-greens, and whether the new proposal should build from it, adapt it, retire it, or leave it separate. Explicitly inspect how a use case imports a rule, whether one-rule-per-file or single-export already exists, how meta-types are represented, and what implementation/domainspec has already developed. Do not edit any file. Return a bounded evidence table, a current enforcement-layer map, and the five most consequential local blind spots.

agents.angle: Ontology and authority: derive candidate implementation-policy types and relationships from DomainSpec v2 while preserving cyberAlchemy-v2 architecture-pattern ontology, authority kinds, source maps, and canonical-versus-generated ownership.
agents.initial_prompt: Read the scoped DomainSpec v2 definitions and relationships, prior language-enforcement and validation findings, and cyberAlchemy-v2 ontology/architecture-pattern/authority surfaces named by the Inventory packet. Propose candidate types and relations for ImplementationProfile, LanguageProjection, ModuleBoundary, RuleDefinition, RuleSet, UseCaseBinding, MetaTypeImplementation, StateMachineContract, Transition, EnforcementObligation, Violation, Suppression, Migration, GeneratedProjection, and EvidenceReceipt only where evidence supports distinct semantics. For each type and edge identify its source authority, lifecycle, canonical versus generated status, invariants, and what must remain language-specific. Test whether style rules such as arrow-functions-only and structural rules such as one-rule-per-file are ontology facts, language-profile policies, or merely local guidelines. Do not promote or edit ontology/authority files. Return a candidate type/relationship table, obligation-to-enforcement-layer map, projection contract, non-collapse list, and blind spots.

agents.angle: Current language implementation: compare official TypeScript, Python, and Rust compiler, linter, import-boundary, custom-rule, state-machine, code-generation, testing, and IDE enforcement capabilities against one shared obligation model.
agents.initial_prompt: Research current TypeScript, Python, and Rust implementation-enforcement practice as of 2026-07-30 using official language, compiler, linter, and tool documentation as primary sources. Compare what belongs in formatter, linter/AST rule, module/import checker, compiler/type checker, schema/graph validator, test harness, code generation, build gate, and runtime assertion. Cover custom-rule extensibility, one-rule-per-file and single-export checks, TypeScript arrow-function policies, Python/Rust idiomatic equivalents or explicit non-equivalence, use-case-to-rule imports, dependency direction, state-machine and typestate patterns, exhaustiveness, concurrency/effects, incremental/IDE feedback, autofix safety, suppressions, generated/vendor/test exclusions, versioning, and CI receipts. Build one capability matrix and propose the smallest toolchain profile per language without installing anything. For each recommendation cite official primary documentation and name limitations, unstable/private APIs, maintenance cost, and when a policy should be killed rather than enforced.

Reconcile the three explorer returns into one exact-bound candidate architecture. Preserve current owners and distinguish observed current state, build-from-owned reuse, proposed additions, deferred questions, and killed ideas. The candidate must include: an enforcement-layer model; candidate ontology types and relationships; canonical/generated/receipt authority table; a universal obligation model plus idiomatic TypeScript/Python/Rust profiles; concrete folder/module/import rules; how a use case binds/imports a rule; how state machines, transitions, effects, and evidence are represented; exception/migration/versioning policy; a minimal cross-language fixture; adoption waves; and a blind-spot register. Every load-bearing row must cite an explorer return and exact source selector or official documentation. Apply the exact-binding contract and emit an evidence-closure candidate matrix; do not write repository files.

groups.anti_bias: Attack-vector axis: precedent and duplicate ownership, executable non-vacuity and counterexample pressure, and definitional plus scope non-collapse.

predicted_disagreements.statement: Agent 0 attacks false novelty and duplicate owners while agent 1 attacks executable non-vacuity and counterexamples on the attack-vector axis; a bias in agent 0 toward build-from-owned reuse would be exposed by agent 1 when existing mechanisms cannot enforce the three-language fixture, while a bias in agent 1 toward adding machinery would be exposed by agent 0 when the compiler, linter, or current DomainSpec validator already owns the obligation.

Agent 0 attacks precedent and ownership duplication while agent 2 attacks definitional and scope collapse on the attack-vector axis; a bias in agent 0 toward reusing one owner would be exposed by agent 2 when style, type, graph, runtime, and authority meanings collapse, while a bias in agent 2 toward multiplying types would be exposed by agent 0 when distinctions add no enforceable behavior.

Agent 1 attacks the candidate with a minimal executable three-language fixture while agent 2 attacks semantic, language-profile, and authority non-collapse on the attack-vector axis; a bias in agent 1 toward a demo-shaped happy path would be exposed by agent 2 when it hides generated-source or suppression semantics, while a bias in agent 2 toward formal cleanliness would be exposed by agent 1 when no real tool can detect the violation with useful diagnostics.

agents.angle: Precedent gate: find the actual local and ecosystem owner for every proposed validator, profile, registry, graph, rule metadata surface, state-machine contract, and receipt; classify build-from-owned versus already-deployed without killing owned candidates.
agents.initial_prompt: Apply the precedent gate to the synthesis. Verify exact local owners in projects/domainspec-v2, implementation/domainspec, cyberAlchemy-v2, and public Arcanum boundaries, then verify external language-tool owners from primary documentation. Detect duplicate sources of truth, second registries, second schedulers/state-machine owners, copied metadata, and proposals that belong as configuration for an existing tool. Return owner citations and build-from-owned/already-deployed/precedent-clean classifications. Precedent never emits KILL; send missing-source defects back through the declared explorer feedback route.

agents.angle: Non-vacuity and counterexample gate: force the proposal through one minimal feature implemented as TypeScript, Python, and Rust projections with an imported rule, state transition, structural failure, semantic failure, suppression, and comparable receipt.
agents.initial_prompt: Apply the non-vacuity gate by constructing the smallest paper-executable cross-language fixture from the synthesis: one use case imports one rule, accepts one input, performs one valid transition, attempts one invalid transition, violates one module boundary, and yields a comparable diagnostic/receipt in TypeScript, Python, and Rust. Include negative controls for an empty rule directory, renamed file, barrel/re-export bypass, dynamic import, generated code, suppression, cyclic dependency, skipped test, and unreachable state. KILL any candidate policy that cannot change an observable verdict, duplicates a compiler guarantee without DomainSpec value, or requires unavailable/unstable tooling without a bounded fallback.

agents.angle: Definitional and scope gate: attack collapses among ontology kind, implementation profile, source module, linter rule, domain rule, state transition, generated projection, runtime behavior, evidence receipt, and promotion authority.
agents.initial_prompt: Apply the definitional-soundness gate. Test whether each proposed type or layer has a distinct owner, invariant, failure mode, and evidence artifact. Reject literal cross-language uniformity where TypeScript arrow functions have no meaningful Python/Rust equivalent; reject folder cleanliness presented as composability proof; reject state-machine diagrams presented as runtime guarantees; reject receipts presented as authority; reject generated code as canonical source; and reject ontology names that merely re-skin existing DomainSpec or cyberAlchemy-v2 concepts. Return explicit KEEP/MERGE/RENAME/DEFER/KILL decisions with cited reasons and the smallest repaired vocabulary.

Write findings.md only from the evidence-closed synthesis and reviewer receipts. Lead with the answer and current-state classification. Include: enforcement layers; candidate ontology and authority map; folder/module/import conventions; rule and meta-type file contracts; use-case and state-machine examples; TypeScript/Python/Rust toolchain matrix; minimum cross-language fixture; adoption/migration waves; developer ergonomics and performance budgets; blind spots and typed negatives; exact source citations; and the required verdict matrix. Clearly label observed, executed, proposed, deferred, killed, and authority-owned claims. Do not write research.md or modify any product, ontology, generated, ledger, Git, or public Arcanum surface.

Audit findings.md only against the frozen goal and exact-binding contract. Require current local selectors, official primary documentation for external tooling, honest authority labels, a complete verdict matrix, one non-vacuous three-language fixture, explicit blind spots, and no claim that research equals implementation or promotion. Reject if style, structural, type, graph, temporal, evidence, or authority layers collapse; if implementation/domainspec precedent is ignored; if a tool is recommended without a maintained extension path; or if the initial profiles are not idiomatic. Return ACCEPT or a bounded writer revision list.
